teaching.en: Each body paragraph starts with a topic sentence that names its main idea.

segments: The rest of the paragraph supports the

es: Enlazar frases sin repetir palabras con this/such, the former/the latter, the same y respectively, y señalar hacia atrás y hacia delante.

teaching.en: Cars and bicycles both create problems: the former pollute the air, and the latter block the pavements.
teaching.es: Los coches y las bicicletas crean problemas: los primeros contaminan el aire y las segundas bloquean las aceras.
teaching.explanationEs: The former = el primero de los dos citados; the latter = el segundo.
segments: Cars and bicycles both create problems: the former pollute
the air, and the latter block the pavements.
teaching.audioText: Cars and bicycles both create problems: the former pollute the air, and the latter block the pavements.

teaching.en: The council banned cars from the centre. This decision surprised many shop owners.
teaching.es: El ayuntamiento prohibió los coches en el centro. Esta decisión sorprendió a muchos comerciantes.
teaching.explanationEs: This + sustantivo resume la idea de la frase anterior sin repetirla.
segments: The council banned cars from the centre.
This decision surprised many shop owners.
teaching.audioText: The council banned cars from the centre. This decision surprised many shop owners.

teaching.en: Such a decision is rarely popular at first, yet the results usually justify it.
teaching.es: Una decisión así rara vez es popular al principio, pero los resultados suelen justificarla.
teaching.explanationEs: Such a + sustantivo = «una … así»; no se dice «such decision» sin artículo.
segments: Such a decision is rarely popular at
first, yet the results usually justify it.
teaching.audioText: Such a decision is rarely popular at first, yet the results usually justify it.

teaching.en: Shop owners and residents asked for parking and quiet, respectively.
teaching.es: Los comerciantes y los vecinos pidieron aparcamiento y silencio, respectivamente.
teaching.explanationEs: Respectively une dos listas en el mismo orden: comerciantes → aparcamiento, vecinos → silencio.
segments: Shop owners and residents asked
for parking and quiet, respectively.
teaching.audioText: Shop owners and residents asked for parking and quiet, respectively.

teaching.en: The buses were late on Monday, and the same happened on Tuesday.

segments: The buses were late on Monday,

teaching.audioText: The buses were late on Monday, and the same happened on Tuesday.

teaching.en: The previous report named two causes; the following sections explain them.

segments: The previous report named two causes;
the following sections explain them.

title.es: Detectar los fallos de un borrador

es: Leer un borrador y localizar repeticiones, referencias ambiguas, saltos lógicos, frases irrelevantes y contradicciones, nombrando cada problema.

teaching.en: This draft is repetitive: the word plan appears in every sentence.
teaching.es: Este borrador es repetitivo: la palabra «plan» aparece en todas las frases.
teaching.explanationEs: Repetitive describe un texto que repite las mismas palabras; draft = borrador.
segments: This draft is repetitive: the word
plan appears in every sentence.
teaching.audioText: This draft is repetitive: the word plan appears in every sentence.

teaching.en: The sentence Ana told Mia she was late is ambiguous: she could be either girl.
teaching.es: La frase «Ana le dijo a Mia que ella llegaba tarde» es ambigua: «ella» puede ser cualquiera de las dos.
teaching.explanationEs: Una referencia es ambiguous cuando un pronombre tiene dos candidatos posibles.
segments: The sentence Ana told Mia she was late
is ambiguous: she could be either girl.
teaching.audioText: The sentence Ana told Mia she was late is ambiguous: she could be either girl.

teaching.en: The writer jumps from rising sales to a failed plan without any logical link.
teaching.es: El autor salta de unas ventas en aumento a un plan fracasado sin ningún vínculo lógico.
teaching.explanationEs: Jumps = salta; falta la razón que conecta dos ideas (un salto lógico).
segments: The writer jumps from rising sales to
a failed plan without any logical link.
teaching.audioText: The writer jumps from rising sales to a failed plan without any logical link.

teaching.en: A sentence about the writer's holiday is irrelevant in a report on school buses.
teaching.es: Una frase sobre las vacaciones del autor es irrelevante en un informe sobre autobuses escolares.
teaching.explanationEs: Irrelevant: no tiene que ver con el tema del texto.
segments: A sentence about the writer's holiday is
irrelevant in a report on school buses.
teaching.audioText: A sentence about the writer's holiday is irrelevant in a report on school buses.

teaching.en: The second sentence contradicts the first, so the paragraph makes no sense.
teaching.es: La segunda frase contradice la primera, así que el párrafo no tiene sentido.
teaching.explanationEs: Contradicts: una frase niega lo que afirmaba otra.
segments: The second sentence contradicts the first,
so the paragraph makes no sense.
teaching.audioText: The second sentence contradicts the first, so the paragraph makes no sense.

teaching.en: Vague words like things and stuff leave the reader unclear about the point.
teaching.es: Palabras vagas como «things» y «stuff» («cosas») dejan al lector sin tener claro el punto.
teaching.explanationEs: Vague = impreciso; unclear = poco claro para el lector.
segments: Vague words like things and stuff leave
the reader unclear about the point.
teaching.audioText: Vague words like things and stuff leave the reader unclear about the point.

es: Escribir un párrafo largo sobre una decisión personal con conectores variados y recortar frases largas sin perder contenido.

teaching.en: Good writers tighten their drafts by cutting every word that adds nothing.
teaching.es: Los buenos escritores ajustan sus borradores eliminando cada palabra que no aporta nada.
teaching.explanationEs: Tighten = apretar el texto: quitar lo que sobra sin perder el contenido.
segments: Good writers tighten their drafts by
cutting every word that adds nothing.
teaching.audioText: Good writers tighten their drafts by cutting every word that adds nothing.

teaching.en: A concise sentence says because where a wordy one says due to the fact that.
teaching.es: Una frase concisa dice «because» donde una verbosa dice «due to the fact that».
teaching.explanationEs: Concise = conciso; wordy = con más palabras de las necesarias.
segments: A concise sentence says because where a wordy
one says due to the fact that.
teaching.audioText: A concise sentence says because where a wordy one says due to the fact that.

teaching.en: She did not make a decision; she decided, and that verb is shorter and stronger.
teaching.es: Ella no tomó una decisión; decidió, y ese verbo es más corto y más fuerte.
teaching.explanationEs: Un verbo fuerte (decided) sustituye a «verbo débil + nombre» (made a decision).
segments: She did not make a decision; she decided,
and that verb is shorter and stronger.
teaching.audioText: She did not make a decision; she decided, and that verb is shorter and stronger.

teaching.en: Redundant words such as very, really and basically can usually be cut.
teaching.es: Las palabras redundantes como very, really y basically casi siempre se pueden eliminar.
teaching.explanationEs: Redundant: no añade información; quitarla no cambia el sentido.
segments: Redundant words such as very, really
and basically can usually be cut.
teaching.audioText: Redundant words such as very, really and basically can usually be cut.

teaching.en: I trimmed the sentence from twenty words to twelve without losing any information.
teaching.es: Recorté la frase de veinte palabras a doce sin perder ninguna información.
teaching.explanationEs: Recortar (trim) es eliminar palabras, no ideas.
segments: I trimmed the sentence from twenty words
to twelve without losing any information.
teaching.audioText: I trimmed the sentence from twenty words to twelve without losing any information.

teaching.en: Admittedly, the course is expensive; nevertheless, it is worth the cost.

teaching.explanationEs: Admittedly concede un punto y nevertheless devuelve la idea principal: conectores variados.
segments: Admittedly, the course is expensive; nevertheless,
it is worth the cost.
teaching.audioText: Admittedly, the course is expensive; nevertheless, it is worth the cost.

prompt.es: Escribe un texto de 130–250 palabras sobre una decisión personal, con conectores.

answer.text: Last year I had to choose between staying in my hometown and studying in another city. Admittedly, staying was the easy option: my family, my friends and my job were all there. Nevertheless, I decided to leave, because I wanted to learn something new. The choice was not simple. I made a list of the advantages and the risks, and I talked to my cousin, who moved abroad two years ago. She told me that the first months are hard, but that the experience changes you. Although I was nervous, I sent my application in March, and I was accepted in June. Now I live in a small flat near the college, and I cook for myself every day. To save money, I work at weekends. I still miss my family, but I do not regret my decision. Looking back, I think that being afraid was normal, and that the important thing was to decide. If I had stayed, I would always have wondered what might have happened.

prompt.es: Escribe un artículo de opinión (130–250 palabras) y termina con «Revision:».

answer.text: Should students have a say in the school rules? In this piece I will argue that they should. First, rules that nobody explains are rarely followed. When students help to write a rule, they understand the reason for it, and they respect it more. Second, taking part teaches responsibility. A student who helps to decide learns that every choice has consequences. I concede that students may not always choose the best rules. Nevertheless, teachers can guide the discussion, and, as mentioned above, a rule with a clear reason is easier to accept. This argument is stronger than the objection, because guided choices are still choices. Teachers and students want different things: the former want order, and the latter want fairness. A shared rule can give both. In conclusion, students deserve a voice in the rules they must follow, and the school will be calmer for it. Do students deserve a say in school rules? I believe they do, and in this piece I will argue it. First, a rule that nobody explains is rarely followed, so students should know why it exists. Second, helping to make rules teaches responsibility, because a student learns that choices have consequences. Admittedly, some students will not choose wisely; nevertheless, teachers can guide them, and, as mentioned above, a clear reason makes any rule easier to accept. This argument answers the objection. Teachers and students often want different things: the former want order, and the latter want fairness, and a shared rule can give both. To sum up, schools should give students a voice, and the result will be a calmer and fairer place. Revision: I changed a long sentence into a shorter one and removed a repeated word.
